passage:
The week before Ganesh Chaturthi: In the maths test, Mridul saw Naveen peek at answers written on his own wrist. Mridul told nobody, but his stomach went tight whenever Naveen walked past.
Thursday, festival art day: The class made paper Ganpati masks. Naveen's had perfect curling trunk lines, and everyone crowded round. "It's copied from somewhere," Mridul muttered, though he had watched Naveen draw every line. When Naveen offered him the gold crayon, Mridul said, "I don't want your stuff."
The next Monday: Naveen's mask was pinned on the notice board with a star beside it. Naveen smiled and waved at Mridul by the water tap. Mridul looked away. "He's only pretending to be nice," he told Kiran.

qa.q: What did Mridul see Naveen do in the maths test?
qa.a: Mridul saw Naveen peek at answers written on his own wrist.

qa.q: Why does Mridul say Naveen is only pretending to be nice?
qa.a: After seeing Naveen cheat, Mridul feels uneasy and distrustful, so even kind acts seem fake; believing Naveen is all bad feels simpler and safer to him.

qa.q: What could help Mridul see Naveen more fairly?
qa.a: An adult or friend could help Mridul look at each thing on its own: the cheating was wrong, but the drawing and the offered crayon were real too.

qa.q: What is it like for Naveen when Mridul looks away?
qa.a: Naveen probably feels confused and hurt, because he was being friendly and doesn't know why Mridul keeps turning away.

grounding: Shows a child who saw a classmate cheat once deciding everything about him is bad, including his drawing and his friendliness.

passage: On cold January mornings the school in Nagaur started at eight, and Sahil arrived with his shawl wrapped twice around his neck. He had walked four kilometres after helping his father milk the goats. "Our sleeper has arrived," Jahnavi ma'am announced, and a few boys laughed. On Friday she returned the essays. Sahil had written three full pages about the camel fair, the best thing he had ever written. Beside his name she had scribbled only, "Margin not drawn. As usual." Gulab's essay, half as long, got "Excellent!" in red. Sahil ran his thumb over his pages. Then he yawned, just once, and Jahnavi ma'am said, "See? Lazy." He folded the essay small and pushed it deep into his bag, under the lunch box his mother had packed at dawn.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi ma'am write beside Sahil's name on the essay?
qa.a: "Margin not drawn. As usual."

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he folded the essay small?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed, because his best writing went unnoticed while the teacher only saw a missing margin and a yawn.

qa.q: How could Jahnavi ma'am see Sahil more fairly?
qa.a: She could read his work without the label in mind, notice the three pages about the camel fair, and ask why he arrives tired before deciding he is lazy.

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi ma'am notice only Sahil's slips?
qa.a: Once she has decided he is lazy, the yawn and the margin fit her label while the long essay does not, so she overlooks it.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelled lazy by a teacher, whose good work is ignored while every small slip is noticed.

passage: During the Diwali break of second year, our group had a design report due, and Kamal sent his section six hours late. I remember sitting on my aunt's terrace with firecrackers going off below, furious, rewriting the introduction so his part would fit. After that I simply stopped giving Kamal anything important. When we planned the final prototype, I gave him the job of buying stationery. When he offered to do the circuit testing, I said, "It's fine, I'll handle it." I told the others he was unreliable, and they believed me. It was only at the end-of-term viva, when Kamal answered the professor's hardest circuit question in two calm lines, that I felt my face go hot. One late file had become everything I thought about him. I'm Anand, and I'm still a bit embarrassed about that semester.

qa.q: How late was Kamal's section of the design report?
qa.a: Six hours late.

qa.q: Why did Anand keep refusing Kamal's offers of help?
qa.a: The late file left Anand angry and distrustful, so relying on Kamal felt risky and doing the work alone felt safer.

qa.q: What could Anand have done after the late file?
qa.a: Anand could have asked Kamal what happened over the break and given him a clear second task, judging him on more than one slip.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt being given only stationery to buy?
qa.a: Kamal likely felt sidelined and frustrated, since he kept offering to do the circuit testing and clearly had the skill for it.

grounding: Shows a student deciding a group member is useless after one late submission and no longer giving him real tasks.

passage:
Mentor's note, Thursday
Aditi came to our check-in upset about Payal, who had sent a client the wrong invoice on Monday. "I can't trust her with the Kolkata account," Aditi said. Then she stopped herself. "Actually, since Monday I've been looking at everything Payal does through that one invoice." I asked what would help. Aditi pulled up Payal's last six months: eleven clean invoices, a client email praising her, and a week when Payal covered two people's work without complaint. She also checked the context: Monday's error came from a template someone else had changed. Aditi decided to keep Payal on the account and fix the template. I suggested she tell Payal both parts, the error and the record. She did, that same afternoon, and came back looking lighter.

qa.q: What mistake did Payal make on Monday?
qa.a: Payal sent a client the wrong invoice.

qa.q: What did Aditi realise about her own view of Payal?
qa.a: Aditi felt uneasy on noticing that she had been seeing everything Payal did through that one invoice, and that her frustration was colouring her judgement.

qa.q: Which steps helped Aditi decide fairly?
qa.a: Looking at Payal's full six-month record and checking the context of the error, which turned out to be a changed template, before deciding about the account.

qa.q: How might Payal feel after hearing both parts from Aditi?
qa.a: Payal is likely relieved and respected, since the mistake was named but her good record was seen too.

grounding: Shows a lead noticing that one error is colouring her view, and reviewing the person's full record and context before deciding.

passage: On the first rainy day of July, everyone crowded into the school corridor because the ground was a lake. I was holding my wet umbrella when Suraj banged into me and my tiffin fell open. "You're so mean!" I shouted. He said sorry, but I didn't listen. I told everyone Suraj was a bully. Ten minutes later I got squashed near the staircase, and my elbow hit a small girl from class two. She started crying. "It wasn't my fault," I told the teacher. "It's so crowded!" At home I told Mummy about both bumps. She raised her eyebrows. "Sumit, so which one of you is mean?" I didn't have an answer. I still don't, really.

qa.q: What happened to Sumit's tiffin?
qa.a: It fell open when Suraj banged into Sumit in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Sumit call Suraj mean but say the second bump wasn't Sumit's fault?
qa.a: Sumit felt the crowd pushing during the second bump but only saw Suraj in the first, so being angry at Suraj felt fair while Sumit felt defensive about the second.

qa.q: What could Sumit ask the next time someone bumps into Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit could ask whether the crowd might have caused it, just like the squash by the staircase, before calling anyone mean.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel after being called a bully?
qa.a: Suraj probably feels hurt and unfairly judged, having said sorry for an accident in a packed corridor.

grounding: Shows a child calling a classmate mean for a bump in a crowded corridor while excusing a similar bump of their own because of the crowd.

passage:
Navratri, day 4
Garba night was amazing except for one thing: Sachin. I messaged him at 6 about going together. Nothing. Called at 7. Switched off. I waited at the gate like an idiot for forty minutes in my new kurta. He saw everything I sent, I bet. He just doesn't care. That's who he is, always doing his own thing. Honestly, I'm done being the one who makes plans.
Told Kunal and Rishi he ditched us. They agreed.
11:50 pm. Sachin's sister just messaged the group: their Nani was taken to hospital this evening, and Sachin's phone died in the rush. He's been in the waiting room all night.
I don't know what to write now. I'm Lalit, the great judge of character, apparently.

qa.q: How long did Lalit wait at the gate?
qa.a: Forty minutes, in a new kurta.

qa.q: Why was Lalit so sure Sachin didn't care?
qa.a: Lalit felt hurt and embarrassed after waiting, and blaming Sachin's character felt natural because the dead phone and the hospital were invisible.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next time before deciding why a friend hasn't replied?
qa.a: List a few possible reasons, like a dead phone or a family emergency, and hold off on telling others until Sachin can explain.

qa.q: What was the evening like for Sachin?
qa.a: Sachin spent it in the hospital waiting room with Nani, phone dead, probably worried and unaware anyone thought he had ditched them.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding a friend who did not reply is uncaring, without imagining a dead phone or a family emergency.

passage: The project was due in thirty-six hours, and the December fog had knocked out power across the hostel block. Akash sat in the dark with a dying laptop, typing furiously in the group chat. "Bhupen missed another morning meeting. Third time. He's just lazy." Two others added thumbs-up. Bhupen's section was half done; his last message had come at 4 am: "will finish by tonight." "Who even works at 4 am?" Akash muttered. "Someone who can't manage time." Near midnight, still without power, Akash walked to the highway petrol pump to find a charging point. Behind the counter of the all-night shop, in a red uniform, stood Bhupen, scanning biscuits for a truck driver. They stared at each other. "Night shift," Bhupen said quietly. "For the fees." Akash's phone buzzed in his pocket. He didn't look at it.

qa.q: Where did Akash find Bhupen near midnight?
qa.a: Behind the counter of the all-night shop at the highway petrol pump.

qa.q: Why did Akash feel sure Bhupen was lazy?
qa.a: Akash was stressed by the deadline and the power cut, and with Bhupen's night shift invisible, missed meetings and 4 am messages seemed to fit only a lazy person.

qa.q: What could Akash have done before calling Bhupen lazy in the chat?
qa.a: Akash could have messaged Bhupen privately to ask what was making mornings hard, and then planned the work around it.

qa.q: What might it be like for Bhupen to read the group chat?
qa.a: Bhupen would likely feel embarrassed and unfairly judged, working night shifts for fees while the group calls him lazy.

grounding: Shows a student calling a groupmate lazy without knowing he works nights, because the hidden pressure is invisible.

passage: Sure, a time I handled a difficult teammate. Last year, at the design studio, Tushar started missing small things: wrong file names, a client call he joined ten minutes late, a typo on a pitch deck. My first thought was, "He's become careless." I actually drafted a message to our manager. Then I deleted it and asked myself what else might be going on. So I took him out for chai and said, "Tushar, the last few weeks look heavy. What's happening?" It turned out his father had moved in with him after surgery, and he was up most nights. But he also admitted he had never liked our file system and had quietly stopped following it. Both things were true. We fixed the naming together, and he moved his calls later for a month. So that's how Rehana handles conflict, I suppose: questions first.

qa.q: What small things did Tushar start missing?
qa.a: Wrong file names, a client call he joined ten minutes late, and a typo on a pitch deck.

qa.q: Why did Rehana delete the message to the manager?
qa.a: Rehana felt curious and a little unsure, wanting to know what else might be happening for Tushar before deciding he was careless 🤔

qa.q: What did asking first achieve?
qa.a: It uncovered both a situation, his father moving in after surgery, and a habit, skipping the file system, so each could be fixed in its own way.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt when Rehana asked what was happening?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt relieved and trusted enough to be honest about both the nights at home and his own habit.

grounding: Shows a colleague asking what might be happening for a teammate before concluding he is careless, and staying open to both a situation and a habit being true.

passage:
Saturday, first week of the summer holidays: Tanvir's team won the gully match by six runs. "That's because I batted like a pro," he told Ira, twirling his bat. "Nobody can bowl to me."
Tuesday: Hot wind blew dust down the lane. Tanvir was out on the second ball, and his team lost. He threw the bat down. "The bat's cracked. And the umpire's blind. That was never out!" Ira, who had been umpiring, crossed her arms.
Friday: Ira drew a chalk line down the wall and wrote two columns, WINS and LOSSES. "So whose fault?" she asked. Tanvir looked at the wall, then at his dusty sandals. "Maybe I swing too early," he mumbled. "Sometimes." He picked up the same bat and asked her to bowl.

qa.q: By how many runs did Tanvir's team win on Saturday?
qa.a: By six runs.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir blame the bat and the umpire on Tuesday?
qa.a: Losing made him feel embarrassed and angry, and blaming the bat and the umpire protected his idea of himself as the best batter.

qa.q: What helped Tanvir look at his own part?
qa.a: Ira's two chalk columns, which made him look at wins and losses the same way and ask whose part each one was.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Tanvir calls the umpire blind?
qa.a: Ira, who was umpiring, likely feels annoyed and unfairly blamed for his loss.

grounding: Shows a child crediting his own skill for a win and blaming the umpire and the bat for a loss.

passage: The half-yearly results came out the week before Eid, when the whole house smelled of sheer khurma and everyone was busy. I got 94 in maths and announced at dinner that I was basically a genius. Then I opened my history paper: 51. I remember saying, "The paper was totally out of syllabus, and ma'am checks too strictly." I said it so often that I believed it. Sunaina, who sits next to me, got 78 in the same paper. "We had the same syllabus, Imran," she said. "You never made notes for the Mughal chapter." I told her she got lucky with the questions. Looking back, it was easier to be a cheated genius than someone who simply hadn't studied. It took me until Diwali to open the Mughal chapter.

qa.q: What did Imran score in history?
Why did Imran blame the paper and the teacher for the history mark?
qa.a: Admitting the missing notes felt embarrassing, so blaming the paper felt comfortable and protected Imran's image as a genius 😅

qa.q: What could Imran do after a low mark instead of blaming the paper?
qa.a: Imran could compare what was studied with the questions asked, like the Mughal chapter, and ask the teacher which areas need work.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see Imran's excuse?
qa.a: Sunaina sees through it, since they had the same syllabus and she knows Imran never made notes for the Mughal chapter.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting brilliance for a high mark and blaming the paper and the teacher for a low one to protect self-image.
